newsitem.title: USA: Biotech vital in feeding world - USDA's Glickman.
newsitem.headline: Biotech vital in feeding world - USDA's Glickman.

text.p: The United States will press for recognition at the World Food Summit of biotechnology's potential to help feed the world, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Friday.
"We need to keep that issue on the table -- what it will do for hungry people," Glickman said at a news conference.

The global conference, which opens Wednesday in Rome, was expected to conclude with a pledge by world leaders to halve the number of hungry people by 2015. About 800 million people are hungry or malnourished now, according to U.N. estimates.
Glickman will lead the U.S. delegation to the meeting.
U.S. firms have been leaders in developing genetically engineered foods. Some of the trail-blazing products -- in corn, wheat and dairy -- have met consumer skepticism.

Biotech foes in Europe demand special labels on foods made with a soybean altered to be herbicide-tolerant. They have campaigned for European Union rejection of corn that produces a biopesticide. Both were genetically engineered in the United States and harvested for the first time this year.

"What we're trying to say at this conference is that biotechnology is an important way to achieve food independence in the developing world as well as (being) economically important to the United States," Glickman said.
"Without it, there are consequences...probably degradation of the environment in order to produce the food that is going to need to be produced."

In a statement, Glickman said the United States would continue to be a leading supplier of food aid. But, he said, "the bulk of the food security burden lies with leaders of the developing world" and they must make sure their policies encourage domestic food production.
He also supported free trade as "the right thing to do in a hungry world" because it would promote investment.
